title: The Fundamental Theorem of Finite Abelian Groups

items.title: Internal direct products of finitely many normal subgroups
items.strategy: Define an internal direct product by generation by the factors together with trivial intersection of each factor with the subgroup generated by all the others. State the binary abelian notation H direct-sum K as the case G=HK and H intersection K is trivial.

items.title: Internal direct products are external direct products, equivalently every element has a unique factorisation
items.strategy: For normal subgroups N_0,...,N_{r-1}, prove that multiplication from their external product to G is a homomorphism because distinct normal factors commute. Identify surjectivity with generation and identify its kernel with the internal intersection conditions. Include the empty family and the binary abelian case.

items.title: The p-primary component of an abelian group
items.strategy: For a prime p define G(p) to be the elements killed by some positive power of p, using multiplicative notation in the statement and recording the equivalent additive notation. Do not assert finiteness or maximality in the definition.

items.title: Cauchy's theorem for finite abelian groups
items.strategy: Induct on the group order. Choose a nontrivial proper cyclic subgroup when the group is not of prime order. Apply induction either in that subgroup or in the abelian quotient; if an order-p quotient element lifts with p-th power of coprime order q, take its q-th power. Treat the trivial and prime-order boundaries explicitly.

items.title: A p-primary component has the full p-power order and is the unique subgroup of that order
items.strategy: Show closure using commutativity. If |G|=p^a m with p not dividing m, prove |G(p)|=p^a: otherwise Cauchy's theorem in G/G(p) supplies a new p-power torsion element. Use Lagrange and the subgroup product formula to prove uniqueness among subgroups of order p^a. Include p not dividing |G|, where G(p) is trivial.

items.title: A finite abelian group is the internal direct product of its primary components
items.strategy: Factor |G| into distinct prime powers. Use Bezout coefficients to express every element as a product of its primary parts, or equivalently use the product map from the primary components. Pairwise coprime orders force trivial intersections, and the order formula gives surjectivity. Cover the trivial group by the empty product convention.

items.title: A nontrivial finite abelian p-group with a unique subgroup of order p is cyclic
items.strategy: Choose an element a of maximal order p^m. If its cyclic subgroup is proper, Cauchy's theorem in the quotient gives b outside it with pb in the cyclic subgroup. Maximality forces the coefficient of a to be divisible by p, making b differ from a multiple of a by an element of the unique order-p subgroup, a contradiction.

items.title: A maximal-order cyclic subgroup splits off a finite abelian p-group
items.strategy: Induct on |G| following Conrad. If G is noncyclic, the preceding lemma gives a second subgroup of order p disjoint from the chosen cyclic subgroup. Pass to its quotient, verify that the image of the chosen generator retains maximal order, split there by induction, and pull the complementary subgroup back. Check the trivial, order-p, and cyclic cases separately.

items.title: Every finite abelian p-group is a direct product of cyclic p-groups
items.strategy: Induct on the group order. Split off a cyclic subgroup generated by an element of maximal order; the complement is a strictly smaller finite abelian p-group unless it is trivial, so induction decomposes it. State the trivial p-group as the empty product.

items.title: Elementary-divisor data for a finite abelian group
items.strategy: Define elementary divisors as the prime powers occurring in a finite external direct-product decomposition into nontrivial cyclic prime-power groups, counted with multiplicity and unordered. Distinguish the data from a choice of internal cyclic subgroups.

items.title: The successive quotients p^iG/p^{i+1}G recover the cyclic summand multiplicities of a finite abelian p-group
items.strategy: For a decomposition into cyclic groups of orders p^{e_j}, compute p^iG componentwise. If |p^iG/p^{i+1}G|=p^{d_i}, show d_i counts exponents e_j at least i+1, so d_{i-1}-d_i counts summands of order p^i. Prove the quotient sizes are intrinsic and include the terminal zero layers.

items.title: Fundamental theorem of finite abelian groups: elementary-divisor form
items.strategy: Use primary decomposition and cyclic decomposition of each p-primary component for existence. For uniqueness, isolate each intrinsic primary component and apply the successive-quotient counts. State uniqueness only up to permutation and isomorphism, never uniqueness of the internal complementary subgroups.

items.title: Invariant-factor data for a finite abelian group
items.strategy: Define an invariant-factor list as positive integers 1<n_1 dividing ... dividing n_r for which G is isomorphic to the product of the cyclic groups of those orders. Exclude unit factors so the list is unique and let the trivial group have the empty list.

items.title: Elementary divisors regroup uniquely into invariant factors
items.strategy: For each prime sort its cyclic exponents in nondecreasing order, left-pad the shorter prime lists with zero exponents, and multiply columnwise. Chinese remainder gives the isomorphism for each column, and the aligned exponents give divisibility. Recover the prime-power columns from any invariant-factor list to prove uniqueness, including the empty list.

items.title: Fundamental theorem of finite abelian groups: invariant-factor form
items.strategy: Apply the elementary-divisor theorem and the regrouping lemma. State the unique empty list for the trivial group and, for a nontrivial group, the unique chain 1<n_1|...|n_r with product |G| and G isomorphic to the product of the corresponding cyclic groups.

items.title: Converse of Lagrange for finite abelian groups: every divisor occurs as a subgroup order
items.strategy: Let d be a positive divisor of |G| and use strong induction on |G|. For d=1 take the trivial subgroup. For d>1 choose a prime p dividing d, use abelian Cauchy to obtain a subgroup H of order p, and apply induction in the finite abelian quotient G/H to the divisor d/p of |G/H|. The full preimage of the resulting subgroup under the quotient map has order d by correspondence and the quotient-order formula. Include the trivial group and d=|G| boundaries explicitly.

items.title: The exponent of a finite group
items.strategy: Define exp(G) as the least positive integer n for which g^n=e for every g in G. Use g^{|G|}=e and well-ordering to justify existence, and set the exponent of the trivial group to one.

items.title: Invariant factors determine the order and exponent of a finite abelian group
items.strategy: For invariant factors n_1|...|n_r, use product cardinality for |G|=n_1...n_r and the direct-product order formula to show exp(G)=n_r when r is nonzero. Check the empty list gives the trivial group of order and exponent one.

items.title: A nontrivial finite abelian group is cyclic if and only if it has one invariant factor
items.strategy: One invariant factor is visibly cyclic. Conversely, classify a finite cyclic group and use uniqueness of invariant factors, or compare its exponent with its order. Keep the trivial group outside the statement because its invariant-factor list is empty.

items.title: Indecomposable and decomposable nontrivial finite abelian groups
items.strategy: Call a nontrivial finite abelian group indecomposable when it is not an internal direct product of two nontrivial subgroups, and decomposable otherwise. Explicitly exclude the trivial group from both labels.

items.title: Every nontrivial finite abelian group is an internal direct product of indecomposable subgroups
items.strategy: Induct on group order. An indecomposable group is the one-factor case; a decomposable group is an internal product B times C of smaller nontrivial groups, whose inductive decompositions concatenate. Use internal-product recognition to pass between nested products.

items.title: The indecomposable finite abelian groups are exactly the nontrivial cyclic groups of prime-power order
items.strategy: The elementary-divisor theorem makes an indecomposable group have one cyclic prime-power factor. Conversely, a cyclic p^a group cannot split into two nontrivial factors because each factor would contain an order-p subgroup while a cyclic group has a unique subgroup of each possible order.

items.title: Partitions of a positive integer
items.strategy: Define a partition of n>0 as a finite nondecreasing list of positive integers whose sum is n. Equality is equality of lists, so order has already been quotiented out by the nondecreasing convention.

items.title: Isomorphism classes of abelian groups of order p^n are counted by partitions of n
items.strategy: Send the nondecreasing list of exponents in the elementary-divisor decomposition to its partition of n. Existence and uniqueness make this a bijection, including n=0 only as the separately stated trivial-group boundary.

items.title: The number of finite abelian groups of order n is the product of the partition numbers of the prime exponents of n
items.strategy: Factor n into prime powers. Primary decomposition makes the choices for distinct primes independent, and the preceding corollary counts the choice for each exponent. State n=1 as one empty choice and avoid any assertion about literal uniqueness of internal subgroups.

items.title: Squarefree positive integers
items.strategy: Define n>0 to be squarefree when no square of a prime divides n, equivalently every exponent in its canonical prime factorisation is zero or one. Record that one is squarefree by the empty factorisation.

items.title: Every abelian group of order n is cyclic if and only if n is squarefree
items.strategy: If n is squarefree, every primary component has prime order and the coprime cyclic factors combine to one cyclic group. If p^2 divides n, use primary decomposition data to construct an abelian group of order n whose p-primary part contains two order-p cyclic factors, so it is not cyclic. Include n=1 explicitly.

title: Finite Abelian Groups: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: The cyclic group of order six in elementary-divisor and invariant-factor forms
items.strategy: Use the Chinese remainder map to identify Z/6 with Z/2 times Z/3. The two prime-order factors are the elementary divisors, while the single factor 6 is the invariant-factor list.

items.title: The five abelian groups of order sixteen
items.strategy: List the five partitions of 4 and translate them into C_16, C_8 times C_2, C_4 times C_4, C_4 times C_2 times C_2, and C_2 to the fourth power. Use uniqueness to show the list has no repetitions and is exhaustive.

items.title: Successive p-multiple layers recover the summands of C_p^2 times C_{p^3} times C_{p^4}^2
items.strategy: Compute the successive layer dimensions as 5,3,3,2,0. Take consecutive differences to recover two order-p summands, no order-p-squared summand, one order-p-cubed summand, and two order-p-fourth summands.

items.title: The six abelian groups of order 360 in both classification forms
items.strategy: Use 360=2^3 times 3^2 times 5. Combine the three partitions of 3 with the two partitions of 2 and the sole partition of 1, list the six elementary-divisor forms, and regroup each into invariant factors.

items.title: Complements of a maximal cyclic subgroup in C_p times C_p need not be unique
items.strategy: Fix one coordinate line in the two-dimensional group over Z/p. Each line of a distinct slope is a complementary order-p subgroup. Verify generation and trivial intersection directly and note that the splitting theorem promises existence, not a canonical complement.

items.title: The unit group modulo one hundred is isomorphic to C_20 times C_2
items.strategy: Verify that the class of 3 has order 20 and the class of -1 has order 2, their cyclic subgroups intersect trivially, and their product has all 40 units. Conclude by internal-product recognition and record invariant factors 2|20.

items.title: The additive rationals do not decompose as a product of finite cyclic prime-power groups
items.strategy: The additive group of rationals is nontrivial and torsion-free: multiplying a nonzero rational by a positive integer never gives zero. Every nontrivial product of finite cyclic prime-power groups has nonzero torsion, so the finite structure theorem cannot be extended by deleting finiteness.

items.title: FALSE: every finite group is a direct product of cyclic prime-power groups
items.strategy: Take a set X with three distinct elements. The symmetric-group lemma gives a group Sym(X) with two explicit noncommuting transpositions, while the finite-bijection theorem gives |Sym(X)|=3!=6. Every cyclic factor is abelian, and componentwise multiplication makes every finite direct product of cyclic groups abelian. Thus this finite nonabelian group cannot have the asserted form.

items.title: The free product of an arbitrary family of groups
items.strategy: Define a free product by its coproduct universal property: compatible data are arbitrary homomorphisms from every factor to one target, with one unique mediating homomorphism. Do not assume the structure maps inject until normal form proves it.

items.title: Reduced syllable words in a family of groups
items.strategy: A syllable is a tagged nonidentity element of one factor. Define a reduced word as a finite syllable list whose adjacent tags differ; the empty word is allowed. Specify elementary multiplication by combining adjacent syllables from the same factor and deleting identities.

items.title: Factor elements act by mutually inverse permutations on reduced syllable words
items.strategy: For g in a factor, define left action on a reduced word by prepending g unless the first syllable lies in the same factor, in which case multiply and delete an identity result. Check all seam cases and prove the action for g^{-1} is inverse. Show each factor map into the permutation group is a homomorphism.

items.title: Reduced syllable words form the free product of a family of groups
items.strategy: Use the factor actions to define multiplication as successive action on the empty word and to separate distinct reduced words. Alternatively describe concatenation followed by seam reduction, then prove associativity through the permutation representation. Evaluate syllables in any target to obtain the unique mediating homomorphism, including the empty family.

items.title: Normal form theorem for free products
items.strategy: Identify the constructed free product with its underlying reduced-word set. Prove every element has one reduced syllable expression and that a nonempty reduced word is not the identity by applying its factor action to the empty word.

items.title: Finite-order elements of a free product are conjugate into factors
items.strategy: Represent a nonidentity element by its reduced syllable word and repeatedly conjugate away matching end-factor syllables until a conjugate is either one syllable or has first and last syllables in different factors. In the latter case every positive power is a nonempty reduced concatenation, so normal form gives infinite order. Hence every nonidentity finite-order element is conjugate to a nonidentity finite-order element of one factor. State the identity separately for a nonempty family and note that the empty-family case is vacuous in the nonidentity formulation.

items.title: The center of a free product with at least two nontrivial factors is trivial
items.strategy: Let z be a nonidentity central element with reduced word x_1...x_n. Choose a nonidentity syllable g from a factor different from the factor of x_1. Then gz is reduced of length n+1. If the last syllable of z lies in g's factor, zg reduces to length at most n; otherwise zg is reduced of length n+1 but starts in a different factor from gz. Normal-form uniqueness gives gz not equal to zg, a contradiction. The identity is central, and the hypothesis supplies the required choice of g even when some other factors are trivial.

items.title: Every canonical factor map into a free product is injective
items.strategy: A nonidentity factor element is a one-syllable reduced word, hence is nonidentity by normal form. Apply the trivial-kernel criterion and include the trivial-factor case.

items.title: Free products are unique up to a unique factor-compatible isomorphism
items.strategy: Use the two universal properties to obtain maps in both directions. Uniqueness makes both composites the identity because they agree with every factor map. Handle the empty family, whose free product is trivial.

items.title: Each factor is a retract of a free product when all other factors are sent trivially
items.strategy: Fix one index. Use the identity on that factor and trivial homomorphisms on all other factors in the universal property, then compose with the injective canonical factor map. State the assertion only for an index belonging to the family.

items.title: A free product has the union presentation of presentations of its factors
items.strategy: After replacing generator alphabets by disjoint copies, show that the group presented by the union of all generators and factor relators has the free-product universal property. Use von Dyck to extend each family of factor maps and uniqueness on generators. Cover empty and singleton families.

items.title: Free groups on disjoint bases freely multiply to the free group on their union
items.strategy: For disjoint sets X_i, compare maps from the union to a target with families of maps from each X_i. The universal properties of the free groups and the free product give the same unique extension, so uniqueness identifies the two groups. Include empty bases and an empty family.

items.title: A free product of copies of the infinite cyclic group is a free group
items.strategy: For each tagged infinite cyclic factor C_i=<c_i>, use the description by integer powers, uniqueness of exponents, and the exponent-addition law to prove directly that (C_i,{x_i}->C_i) satisfies the free-group universal property on the singleton {x_i}. Make the singleton bases disjoint and apply the disjoint-basis theorem. Preserve the arbitrary index set and its empty case.

items.title: The free product of two infinite cyclic groups is the free group on two generators
items.strategy: Specialise the preceding arbitrary-family result to two singleton bases and use the finite-rank definition. Record the compatible images of the two standard generators.

items.title: Pushouts of group homomorphisms
items.strategy: For homomorphisms f:K to G and h:K to H, define a group pushout by the commuting-square universal property. Do not build injectivity into the definition and explicitly allow arbitrary, noninjective homomorphisms.

items.title: A group pushout is the quotient of a free product by the amalgamating relations
items.strategy: Form G*H and quotient by the normal closure of f(k)h(k)^{-1} for k in K. The quotient maps agree on K. Given any compatible pair of maps, free-product universality supplies a map that kills those relators, so quotient universality gives the unique mediator. Include K, G, or H trivial and arbitrary kernels.

items.title: Free products with amalgamation along monomorphisms
items.strategy: When f:K to G and h:K to H are injective, call their group pushout the free product with amalgamation G *_K H. Explain that the notation identifies K with its two images only after the embedding theorem is proved.

items.title: A free product with amalgamation has the factor presentations plus the amalgamating relations
items.strategy: Take disjoint presentations of G and H, use their union presentation for G*H, and add relations identifying a chosen generating set of K through the two monomorphisms. Prove the resulting presentation has the pushout universal property and explain why using all k in K gives the same normal closure.

items.title: Transversal normal-form data for an amalgamated free product
items.strategy: After identifying K with subgroups of G and H provisionally, choose left-coset transversals S_G,S_H containing the identity. Define normal words s_1...s_n k with nonidentity representatives alternating between transversals and k in K. Record length zero and the dependence of the written representative on the transversal choices.

items.title: Factor elements act consistently by permutations on amalgamated normal words
items.strategy: Following Schreier's permutation proof, define P_g(w) by multiplying the terminal K coefficient on the right by g^{-1}, rewriting uniquely with the selected left-coset transversal, and merging with the last syllable when it comes from the same factor. Check P_{gh}=P_g composed with P_h under the library's composition convention, prove inverses act inversely, and prove that the two factor actions agree on K.

items.title: Normal form theorem for free products with amalgamation
items.strategy: Use the factor actions to realise the presented amalgamated product as permutations of its normal-word set. Show every element has a unique form s_1...s_n k and that a positive-length normal word is nonidentity. Prove independence of the chosen transversals through the pushout universal property, while retaining the length-zero K case.

items.title: The factor maps into a free product with amalgamation are injective
items.strategy: A nonidentity element of either factor has either a nontrivial K coefficient or a one-syllable normal form, so it cannot map to the identity. Apply the trivial-kernel criterion and keep the trivial factor and K=G boundary cases.

items.title: The two factor images intersect exactly in the amalgamated subgroup
items.strategy: The amalgamated K-image lies in both factors. Conversely, if images of g in G and h in H agree, the normal form of gh^{-1} can be trivial only when both elements represent the same element of K. Include K trivial and K equal to one factor.

items.title: Amalgamation over the trivial group is the ordinary free product
items.strategy: For the two maps from the trivial group, the compatibility condition is automatic, so the pushout and free-product universal properties coincide. Use uniqueness to obtain the canonical isomorphism and check trivial factors.

items.title: The kernels of the amalgamating maps are killed in the opposite canonical maps to a group pushout
items.strategy: If k lies in ker f, commutativity gives i_H(h(k))=i_G(e)=e; symmetrically i_G(f(ker h)) is trivial. Deduce that injectivity of a canonical factor map can fail for arbitrary pushout data and identify the exact kernel containment without claiming equality.

items.title: A pushout along an isomorphism is isomorphic to the other factor
items.strategy: When f:K to G is an isomorphism, use h composed with f^{-1}:G to H and the identity of H as a compatible cocone. Verify the universal property and obtain the unique isomorphism. Treat trivial groups without a separate argument.

items.title: Conventions and proved scope for free products and amalgamation
items.strategy: Record that free products allow arbitrary index sets; group pushouts allow arbitrary homomorphisms; the notation G *_K H and the normal-form, embedding, and intersection theorems require monomorphisms. State that HNN extensions, Kurosh's subgroup theorem, Grushko's theorem, and Bass-Serre theory are not claimed from this page's declared prerequisites.

items.title: C_2 free-product C_2 is the infinite dihedral group, and the product of its generators has infinite order
items.strategy: Use the union presentation to obtain generators s,t with s^2=t^2=e. Normal form shows every positive power of st is a nonempty reduced word, so st has infinite order. Identify this presentation as the standard infinite dihedral group convention.

items.title: C_2 free-product C_3 has presentation with only the two factor relations and is infinite
items.strategy: The presentation theorem gives <s,t | s^2, t^3>. The words (st)^n are distinct reduced normal forms for nonnegative n, proving infinitude without importing the modular-group identification.

items.title: The canonical surjection from a free product to the direct product of its factors
items.strategy: Map G to G times H by g to (g,e) and H by h to (e,h), then use free-product universality. These images generate the direct product, so the induced map is surjective. Show every cross-commutator lies in its kernel and give nontrivial factors for which normal form makes such a commutator nonidentity.

items.title: FALSE: a free product of abelian groups is abelian
items.strategy: In C_2*C_2 the reduced words st and ts are distinct. Thus the two canonical generators do not commute even though both factors are abelian.

items.title: Amalgamating infinite cyclic groups by multiplication by m and n gives the presentation with relation x^m=y^n
items.strategy: For positive m,n, realise each factor as the one-generator word-quotient free group. Its normal form shows that it is infinite cyclic, and the free-group theorem together with the presentation definition and the empty normal closure gives its empty-relator presentation. Apply the amalgamated-presentation theorem to the injective maps taking the edge generator to x^m and y^n. The amalgam normal form embeds both cyclic factors. Specialise to m=2,n=3 without asserting the torus-knot interpretation.

items.title: Amalgamating C_2 inside C_4 and C_6 gives the presentation with a^2=b^3
items.strategy: Embed C_2 as the unique order-two subgroup in each cyclic factor. The presentation is <a,b | a^4, b^6, a^2=b^3>. Apply embedding and intersection corollaries to verify that the factor images remain C_4 and C_6 and meet in precisely C_2.

items.title: FALSE: canonical factor maps into every group pushout are injective
items.strategy: Take the maps from C_2 to the trivial group and to C_2, the first trivial and the second the identity. The pushout is trivial by its universal property, so the canonical map from the second C_2 is not injective. Relate this directly to kernel collapse.

items.title: Amalgamating along a whole factor recovers the other group
items.strategy: For an isomorphism K to G and any homomorphism K to H, construct the pushout as H. Work one concrete cyclic case and check both legs and the unique mediator rather than appealing only to the slogan.
